newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT - T-bonds steamroll ahead, look to 117-00.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT - T-bonds steamroll ahead, look to 117-00.

text.p: September U.S. Treasury bond futures stampeded higher Wednesday in a display of such bullish resolve that technicians for now have shelved concerns about the contract's highly overbought status.
"It's feeling like a freight train running and I don't know what's going to stop it," said Steven Poser, senior technical analyst with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Poser said September bonds would likely trade in the 117-00 handle before registering a short-term top.
"This is as violent and sustainable and as mature an uptrend as we've seen in a long time," said Dave Toth, analyst with Optima Institutional Services.
"At this juncture, there is no objective technical reason to believe this rally is done."
Sentiment indicators show bulls haven't been as wildly optimistic since October 1995, Toth said, yet that rally continued for another five points before peaking.
Market participants are now eyeing 116-28/32, the high from December 1996 on continuation charts.
The level is significant because it is a previous battleground but needn't stop the bull run this time, Toth said.
"At this point, the upside is totally indeterminable," said the analyst.
A relapse below old resistance levels such as 115-16/32 or 114-30/32 would be necessary to cast doubt on the market's ability to register still-higher highs, he said.
For December Eurodollar futures, he added, a pullback below 94.13 or 94.09 in the short term would be needed.

Poser said Friday appears on Elliott Wave radar screens as a possible date for a correction based on time-series analysis, noting that happens to be when the Labor Department is releasing July U.S. employment data.
He emphasized the market could shed three points in a correction, then turn around and continue making new highs.

At the short end, Poser said 5.70-5.71 percent was a key yield target on the two-year note. The yield hit a low of 5.71 percent in February, while 5.70 percent is the midpoint between the April 1993 yield low and December 1994 yield high.
The two-year is currently yielding 5.76 percent.
